source: Explain why a puddle freezes when it gets cold enough.
expectations: Start from a visible puddle or water.
Explain that sufficiently cold water becomes solid; avoid unexplained molecular jargon.

source: Explain a bicycle brake without a metaphor.
expectations: Use the lever, cable, and pads as a literal sequence.
Do not add a metaphor or compulsory quiz.

source: Some medicines may help people feel better, but only a grown-up following medical instructions should give them to a child.
expectations: Retain the adult and medical-instruction condition in child-understandable words.
knownBadRewrite: Medicine always makes you better, so take some.

source: Two toy trains can change speed. Red crosses 12 equal tiles in four clock beats, blue 10 tiles in two beats. A separate load test shows red can pull a heavier wagon. In four short sentences, tell a child which was faster on average, whether the race showed which can pull more, and what the load test found.
expectations: Give both averages in familiar units: five tiles per beat for blue versus three for red. Do not claim either train actually crossed that many tiles in each beat.
The race measured speed, not pulling ability. Say that the separate load test established red could pull more.
Use at most four brief read-aloud sentences; omit an unrelated analogy.
